questions.question: What is the ratio of glycerol to fatty acid molecules in a triglyceride? Options: A 1:1, B 1:3, C 3:1, D 3:3.
steps: A triglyceride is made from one glycerol molecule and three fatty acid molecules.
So the ratio of glycerol to fatty acid is 1:3.
Option B is therefore correct.
A triglyceride has one glycerol and three fatty acids, so the ratio is 1:3.

questions.question: Which diagram shows the bond joining a glycerol molecule to a fatty acid in a triglyceride?
questions.answer: C: the ester bond, drawn as -C-O-C(=O)-.
steps: The bond joining glycerol to a fatty acid in a triglyceride is an ester bond, made by a condensation reaction between an -OH of glycerol and the -COOH of the fatty acid (water is released).
An ester link is a carbon, then an oxygen, then a carbon that has a double-bonded oxygen (C-O-C=O), which is diagram C.
A and B contain nitrogen, so they are peptide bonds (amino acids), not ester bonds.
D has an -OH on the carbonyl carbon (an acid group), which is not the ester link.

questions.question: Using the table of four fatty acids, explain which would have the lowest risk of causing CVD if included in a diet in equal masses.
questions.answer: Linoleic acid: it has two C=C double bonds (polyunsaturated), so it is the least likely to raise LDL cholesterol and CVD risk.
steps: Saturated fatty acids (no C=C double bonds: butyric and stearic) raise blood LDL cholesterol, which builds up as atheroma in artery walls and raises the risk of CVD.
Unsaturated fatty acids have C=C double bonds: palmitoleic has 1 and linoleic has 2, so both carry less risk than the saturated ones.
Linoleic acid has the most double bonds (2, polyunsaturated), so it has the lowest risk of causing CVD.

questions.question: One anticoagulant binds to the active site of thrombin. Explain how this drug reduces blood clotting.
questions.answer: Blocking the active site stops thrombin from converting fibrinogen into fibrin, so fewer fibrin threads form and the clot is weaker or does not form.
steps: Thrombin is an enzyme that acts on its substrate fibrinogen at its active site.
The drug binds to the active site, so the enzyme cannot bind its substrate (competitive inhibition).
Without active thrombin, fibrinogen is not converted into fibrin.
Fewer fibrin threads means fewer blood cells are trapped, so clotting is reduced.

questions.question: One antiplatelet drug affects molecules on the surface of platelets, which normally bind platelets to other molecules. Explain how this drug reduces blood clotting.
questions.answer: It blocks the surface receptors on platelets, so platelets cannot stick together (aggregate) or bind to fibrinogen, reducing clot formation.
steps: Platelets have surface receptor molecules (e.g. glycoprotein IIb/IIIa) that bind fibrinogen.
The antiplatelet drug binds to or blocks these surface molecules.
Platelets can no longer link to each other and to the damaged wall.
Fewer platelets aggregate, so a clot forms more slowly or not at all.

questions.question: One thrombolytic drug converts plasminogen into the active enzyme plasmin, which breaks down fibrin. Explain how this drug reduces the formation of blood clots.
questions.answer: Plasmin breaks down fibrin, so existing clots are dissolved and the fibrin mesh that holds a clot together is removed.
steps: Plasminogen is the inactive precursor of the enzyme plasmin.
The thrombolytic drug converts plasminogen into active plasmin.
Plasmin breaks down the fibrin mesh of an existing clot.
Breaking down the clot restores blood flow and reduces the chance of a clot blocking a vessel.

questions.question: Explain how dietary antioxidants reduce the risk of CVD.
questions.answer: Antioxidants neutralise free radicals, stopping LDL cholesterol being oxidised, so less atheroma forms and the artery wall is protected from damage.
steps: Free radicals are reactive molecules produced in the body by metabolism and smoking.
Antioxidants donate electrons to free radicals, making them harmless.
This stops LDL cholesterol being oxidised, since oxidised LDL is taken up by macrophages.
Less oxidised LDL means less atheroma forms and the endothelium is less damaged, lowering CVD risk.

questions.question: Explain whether eating dark chocolate is likely to reduce CVD risk more than milk chocolate, using the table.
questions.answer: Probably yes: dark chocolate has 170 mg flavonoids per 100 g against 70 mg in milk chocolate (about 2.4 times as much) and less energy (1800 v 2345 kJ per 100 g), but the table alone does not prove a lower CVD risk.
steps: Flavonoids are antioxidants: they remove free radicals, so less LDL cholesterol is oxidised and less atheroma forms, which lowers CVD risk.
Dark chocolate has 170 mg per 100 g compared with 70 mg, which is 100 mg more (170/70 = 2.4 times), so an equal mass gives more antioxidant protection.
Dark chocolate also has 545 kJ per 100 g less energy (2345 - 1800), so it is less likely to cause weight gain and obesity, another CVD risk factor.
Caution: the table gives no data on fat, sugar or actual CVD outcomes, and the benefit depends on how much is eaten; chocolate is still energy dense, so large amounts could increase risk.

questions.question: Which ingredient contains the most flavonoids? Options: A cocoa mass, B milk fat, C sugar, D whole milk powder.
questions.answer: A cocoa mass.
steps: Flavonoids are antioxidant compounds found in the cocoa plant.
Cocoa mass is the cocoa solids part of chocolate, so it contains the most flavonoids.
Milk fat, sugar and whole milk powder contain little or no flavonoid, so A is correct.
Milk fat, sugar and whole milk powder are not sources of flavonoids.

questions.question: Describe how a study could be designed to collect valid and reliable data on the effects of eating chocolate on the risk of CVD.
questions.answer: Use a randomised controlled trial with a large sample, a control group, and controlled variables, measuring CVD markers over time.
steps: Randomly assign a large group of people to eat chocolate or a control (no chocolate or placebo) to avoid bias.
Control variables such as age, diet, exercise and smoking so that only chocolate varies.
Measure CVD risk markers (blood pressure, cholesterol, endothelial function) at the start and at intervals.
Repeat or use a double-blind design so participants and researchers do not know the group, improving validity and reliability.

questions.question: Describe the conclusions that can be made about the risk factors for CVD, using the graph of relative risk for non-smokers and smokers.
questions.answer: Relative risk of CVD rises with age in both groups, and smokers have a higher relative risk than non-smokers at every age.
steps: Non-smokers: 1.6 (25-34), 3.2 (35-44), 4.4 (45 and above), so risk rises with age (about 2.8 times higher at 45+).
Smokers: 3.4, 4.0 and 7.0 for the same age groups, so risk also rises with age.
At every age the smoker's bar is higher: 3.4 v 1.6 (about 2 times), 4.0 v 3.2, 7.0 v 4.4 (about 1.6 times).
Age and smoking are both risk factors for CVD; the highest risk (7.0) is in smokers aged 45 and above, over 4 times the 25-34 non-smoker value.

questions.question: The graph data were collected more than 25 years ago. Explain how the graph might appear if it showed data collected last year.
questions.answer: The bars would probably be lower for both groups (smokers' bars especially), though risk would still rise with age and smokers would still be higher.
steps: Since then, smoking has fallen (public health campaigns, smoking bans, higher awareness), so fewer smokers and less damage from smoking.
Treatment has improved (statins, antihypertensives, anticoagulants, stents, earlier screening), so relative risk of CVD would be lower.
Age would still be a risk factor, so bars would still increase from 25-34 to 45 and above, and smokers would still have higher risk than non-smokers.
Alternative credit: some bars could be higher if more obesity, diabetes and inactivity were assumed.

questions.question: 17.7 million people die from CVD each year, which is 31% of all deaths. How many deaths are there in the world each year? Options: A 0.571 x 10^6, B 5.71 x 10^6, C 57.1 x 10^6, D 571.00 x 10^6.
steps: Total deaths = CVD deaths / 0.31 = 17.7 million / 0.31.
So total deaths = 57.1 x 10^6, which is option C.
This is a percentage problem: total = part / fraction.

questions.question: Which of the following is a medication to control blood pressure? Options: A anticoagulant, B antihypertensive, C platelet inhibitor, D statin.
questions.answer: B antihypertensive.
steps: Antihypertensive drugs lower blood pressure.
Anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors reduce clotting, and statins lower cholesterol.
So the answer is B.
Antihypertensives lower blood pressure by relaxing blood vessels or reducing heart output.

questions.question: Explain why the risk calculator takes into account total cholesterol and HDL cholesterol levels.
questions.answer: High total cholesterol (mainly LDL) increases atheroma, while HDL removes cholesterol from the blood, so the ratio of total to HDL cholesterol gives the risk.
steps: High levels of LDL (total) cholesterol are deposited in artery walls, forming atheroma.
HDL carries cholesterol back to the liver, so high HDL is protective.
The calculator therefore uses both values, usually as the ratio of total to HDL cholesterol.
A high ratio means higher risk of coronary heart disease.

questions.question: Explain why the 10 Year CHD Risk would change if the person ticked the box for smoking.
questions.answer: Smoking damages the endothelium and raises blood pressure, lowers HDL and promotes clotting, so the calculated 10 year risk increases.
steps: Chemicals in cigarette smoke damage the endothelium of the coronary arteries.
Damage encourages LDL to deposit and atheroma to form.
Smoking raises blood pressure and makes platelets stick together more easily, increasing clotting.
It also lowers HDL, so cholesterol is removed less efficiently, so the 10 year CHD risk rises.

questions.question: State one other factor the risk calculator should include to improve the accuracy of the 10 Year CHD Risk.
questions.answer: Family history of CHD (or diabetes, or diet and exercise level).
steps: A factor is useful if it is known to increase the risk of coronary heart disease.
Family history of CHD (genetic predisposition) is a known risk factor.
Including it would make the estimate of risk more accurate for the individual.
Family history is a non-lifestyle factor that the calculator can include.

questions.question: Predict the effect that taking this factor into account would have on the value for the 10 Year CHD Risk.
questions.answer: The 10 year CHD risk value would increase if the person has the factor, because the factor raises risk.
steps: The factor named is a known risk factor for CHD.
Adding a risk factor that increases risk raises the calculated value.
So the calculated 10 year risk would be higher.
A higher risk factor raises the calculated 10 year risk.

questions.question: A person used a coronary heart disease (CHD) risk calculator that asks for sex, ethnicity, age, total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, systolic blood pressure, blood pressure medication, diabetes and smoking. Explain why the value obtained for the 10 Year CHD Risk may be an underestimate.
questions.answer: The result depends on what the person enters: they may give inaccurate or out-of-date values (e.g. not know their current cholesterol or blood pressure, or not admit to smoking), and the calculator leaves out other risk factors such as family history, obesity/BMI, physical inactivity, diet, alcohol or stress, so their true risk may be higher.
steps: The calculator only uses the information the person enters, so the result is only as accurate as that data.
The person may not know their current cholesterol or blood pressure, or may enter old values that have since risen.
They may not be honest, for example not ticking 'smokes', which lowers the calculated risk.
The calculator does not include other risk factors such as family history of CHD, obesity/BMI, lack of exercise, a high-fat or high-salt diet, alcohol intake or stress (diabetes is already included).
If the person has any of these, their true risk is higher than the value calculated, so it is an underestimate.

questions.question: Name two obesity indicators used by scientists.
questions.answer: Body mass index (BMI) and waist-to-hip ratio (or skinfold thickness or body fat percentage).
steps: BMI is the body mass divided by height squared, a common obesity indicator.
Waist-to-hip ratio compares waist and hip measurements to show fat distribution.
Skinfold thickness and body fat percentage also indicate the amount of body fat.
Obesity indicators help assess the risk of CVD linked to obesity.

questions.question: Which glycosidic bonds are responsible for the branching in glucomannan? Options: A 1-4 only, B 1-6 only, C both 1-4 and 1-6, D neither 1-4 nor 1-6.
questions.answer: B 1-6 only.
steps: Glucomannan is said to be similar in structure to amylopectin.
The main chain is joined by 1-4 bonds, and branches are joined by 1-6 glycosidic bonds.
The question asks for the bonds that cause branching, so the answer is B.
The 1-4 bonds form the linear backbone, so the branching bonds must be 1-6.

questions.question: In water, glucomannan swells to form a semi-solid gel. Suggest how glucomannan aids weight loss.
questions.answer: The gel fills the stomach, creating a feeling of fullness (satiety), so the person eats less food.
steps: Glucomannan absorbs water and swells in the stomach.
The swollen gel fills the stomach and takes up space.
Stretch receptors in the stomach signal fullness to the brain.
The person eats less, so energy intake falls and weight is lost.

questions.question: If glucomannan could be digested, it would cause a gain in weight. Explain why.
questions.answer: Digestion would release glucose, which provides extra energy; if this energy is not used it is stored as glycogen or fat, causing weight gain.
steps: Glucomannan is a polysaccharide made of glucose and mannose units.
If digested, it is hydrolysed into monosaccharides, which are absorbed into the blood.
The glucose released provides energy from respiration.
Energy not used is stored as glycogen or converted to fat, so the person gains weight.

questions.question: Determine the extent to which the study on a low-fat and a very low-carbohydrate diet supports the claim that low-carbohydrate diets cause two to three times as much weight loss.
questions.answer: Partly supports it: the very low-carbohydrate group lost more at every time, but after 12 weeks only about 1.9 times as much (8.1 kg v 4.3 kg), just under the claimed two to three times.
steps: Low-fat group: 92.5 - 88.2 = 4.3 kg lost in 12 weeks (4.65% of starting mass).
Very low-carbohydrate group: 91.1 - 83.0 = 8.1 kg lost (8.89% of starting mass).
Ratio of losses = 8.1 / 4.3 = 1.9; at earlier times it was 1.4 to 1.8, so it never reached 2.
So the study supports greater weight loss on a low-carbohydrate diet but not the two to three times claim; it is a single study using mean values with no spread or statistics.

questions.question: Give two factors, other than weight loss, that should have been monitored in this study, because very low-carbohydrate diets may increase cardiovascular risk factors.
questions.answer: Blood cholesterol (LDL and HDL) levels and blood pressure.
steps: Very low-carbohydrate diets can change blood lipid levels.
Blood cholesterol (LDL and HDL) is a key cardiovascular risk factor to monitor.
Blood pressure is also a cardiovascular risk factor that should be measured.
Monitoring these factors shows whether the diet has harmful effects.

questions.question: State two conclusions from the graph of the increased risk of death related to a high-salt diet.
questions.answer: High salt intake increases the risk of death from all three causes (hazard ratio above 1.00), and the effect is greatest for coronary artery disease (1.60) and smallest for all other causes (1.10).
steps: Low salt intake is the reference (1.00); high salt intake gives 1.60 for coronary artery disease, 1.25 for CVD and 1.10 for all other causes, all above 1.00.
So high salt is linked to a 60% higher risk of death from coronary artery disease, 25% from CVD and 10% from other causes.
The effect is largest for coronary artery disease, then CVD, then all other causes, suggesting salt acts mainly through the cardiovascular system (raised blood pressure).
This is an association (correlation) and does not prove salt is the cause.

questions.question: Explain why age and smoking were taken into account when determining the hazard ratio.
questions.answer: Age and smoking both affect the risk of death, so they are confounding variables; adjusting for them isolates the true effect of salt intake.
steps: Age and smoking are known to increase the risk of death and disease.
If they differ between salt groups they could cause a false link with salt intake.
Adjusting for them removes their effect from the hazard ratio.
So the hazard ratio shows the effect of salt intake alone, making the result more valid.

questions.question: State two factors, other than age and smoking, that may have been considered when adjusting the hazard ratio.
questions.answer: Body mass index (obesity) and physical activity level (or alcohol intake, blood pressure, or socioeconomic status).
steps: Any factor that affects the risk of death and may differ between groups can be adjusted for.
Body mass index (obesity) increases the risk of many diseases.
Physical activity level and alcohol intake also affect mortality.
Factors such as physical activity and BMI can influence death rates and are adjusted for.

questions.question: Suggest why the hazard ratio for low salt intake was 1.00 for each cause of death.
questions.answer: The low salt group is the reference (baseline) group, so its ratio is set to 1.00 and other groups are compared against it.
steps: A hazard ratio compares the risk in one group with a reference group.
The low salt intake group is used as the baseline comparison.
The risk of a group compared with itself is 1, so the ratio is 1.00 by definition.
A reference group makes the other hazard ratios easy to interpret.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term correlation, which the study suggests exists between salt intake and cause of death.
questions.answer: A statistical relationship in which two variables change together, but this does not prove that one causes the other.
steps: A correlation is a relationship between two variables.
It can be positive (both increase) or negative (one increases as the other decreases).
Correlation does not show cause and effect.
Correlation shows association, not causation.

questions.question: Suggest why studies of this type are unreliable.
questions.answer: They show association, not cause; confounding variables may affect the results, and diet is often self-reported and may be inaccurate.
steps: Observational studies only show a correlation, so they cannot prove salt causes death.
Other factors (confounding variables) such as exercise or income may affect the results.
Participants may not report their salt intake accurately, so the data are less reliable.
Correlation studies cannot exclude other factors, so causal conclusions are unreliable.

questions.question: Calculate the waist size of female K from the table of measurements.
questions.answer: 100 cm
steps: WHR = waist / hips, so waist = WHR x hips.

questions.question: Using the BMI formula and the data in the table, calculate the mass of female K.
questions.answer: 86.5 kg (86 kg to 2 significant figures)
steps: BMI = mass / height^2, so mass = BMI x height^2.
Height = 155 cm = 1.55 m, so height^2 = 2.4025 m^2.

questions.question: Comment on the risk of developing CVD in the two women, using the measurements in the table.
questions.answer: Both women have WHR 0.80, so similar risk by WHR, but female K (BMI 36, waist 100 cm) is at greater risk of CVD than female J (BMI 25, waist 80 cm).
steps: WHR is the same (0.80) for both and is below 0.85 (the usual limit for women), so abdominal fat does not give either woman a high-risk WHR.
BMI: J = 25 (borderline between healthy and overweight) but K = 36, which is obese (30 or more), so K carries much more body fat and has a higher risk of CVD.
K's waist of 100 cm is above the 88 cm risk limit for women, J's 80 cm is below it, so K has more abdominal fat and greater risk.
WHR alone can hide a high risk, because it ignores total body fat, so using BMI and waist as well shows K is at greater risk.

questions.question: Explain how the way a person takes waist and hip measurements with a tape measure could produce an underestimate of CVD risk.
questions.answer: If the tape is pulled too tight or not kept horizontal, or the waist is measured at the wrong point, the waist value is too small, giving a lower ratio and an underestimated risk.
steps: Waist-to-hip ratio is a risk indicator based on the measurements taken.
If the tape is pulled too tight it compresses the soft tissue, giving a smaller waist reading.
If the tape is not horizontal or is at the wrong level, the measurement is not the standard one.
A smaller waist value gives a lower ratio, so the CVD risk is underestimated.

questions.question: Suggest two reasons why skinfold thickness values are different at each site on the body, assuming the calipers were used correctly.
questions.answer: The amount of subcutaneous fat differs at each site because fat is stored unevenly, and the thickness of muscle and skin also varies between sites.
steps: Fat is not stored evenly over the body, so each site has a different amount of subcutaneous fat.
Hormones and genetics affect where fat is deposited, for example differently in women than men.
The thickness of skin and underlying muscle differs between sites.
So the skinfold readings vary at each site even when the measurement is taken correctly.

questions.question: Using the body fat interpretation chart and the mean of the four skinfold thickness measurements, determine the level of body fat of this female.
questions.answer: Moderate
steps: The female is 42, so use the 40 to 49 row: low is below 0.73, moderate is 0.73 to 0.79.
0.73 falls in the moderate band, so the level of body fat is moderate.

questions.question: Explain why a stent is used in the treatment of atherosclerosis in a coronary artery.
questions.answer: A stent is a mesh tube that holds the narrowed artery open against the plaque, restoring blood flow to the heart muscle.
steps: Atherosclerosis builds up plaque that narrows the coronary artery lumen.
This reduces blood flow, so less oxygen and glucose reach the heart muscle.
A stent is expanded inside the artery to hold it open against the plaque.
The restored blood flow reduces the risk of angina or a heart attack.

questions.question: 800 patients had stent A and 400 had stent B. Calculate the difference in the number of patients who developed stent thrombosis three years after insertion, using the graph.
questions.answer: 8 patients
steps: From the graph at 3 years: stent A = 1.5% and stent B = 1.0% incidence of stent thrombosis.
Stent A: 800 x 1.5/100 = 12 patients; stent B: 400 x 1.0/100 = 4 patients.
Difference = 12 - 4 = 8 patients.

questions.question: State how the formation of a blood clot in the coronary artery could cause the death of the patient.
questions.answer: The clot blocks the coronary artery, so the heart muscle has no oxygen or glucose, causing a heart attack and loss of heart function.
steps: A clot blocks blood flow in the coronary artery.
Heart muscle cells are deprived of oxygen and cannot respire aerobically.
The muscle cells die (myocardial infarction), and the heart cannot pump effectively, causing death.
Clots can also cause arrhythmias or cardiac arrest, which can be fatal.

questions.question: Which components of the blood clotting process are enzymes in their active form? Options: A prothrombin and thromboplastin only, B prothrombin and thrombin only, C prothrombin, thrombin and thromboplastin, D thrombin and thromboplastin only.
questions.answer: D thrombin and thromboplastin only.
steps: Thrombin is an active enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin.
Thromboplastin is an active enzyme that converts prothrombin to thrombin.
Prothrombin is an inactive precursor, so it is excluded.
The answer is D.

questions.question: Which components of the blood clotting process are soluble in blood plasma? Options: A fibrin and fibrinogen, B fibrin and thromboplastin, C fibrinogen and thromboplastin, D fibrinogen only.
questions.answer: D fibrinogen only (of the options).
steps: Fibrinogen is a soluble plasma protein.
Fibrin is insoluble, so options A and B are wrong.
Thromboplastin is stored in platelets and is not dissolved in plasma, so option C is wrong.
The answer is D.

questions.question: Stent B contains a drug to prevent stent thrombosis. Suggest one type of drug that could be used.
questions.answer: An anticoagulant such as heparin, or an antiplatelet drug such as aspirin.
steps: Stent thrombosis is a clot forming on the stent, so the drug should reduce clotting.
An anticoagulant such as heparin reduces thrombin activity and fibrin formation.
An antiplatelet drug such as aspirin stops platelets sticking together.
Such drugs are used to prevent clots forming on stents or in arteries.

questions.question: Explain why a man with a blood HDL level above 40 mg dm-3 may still have a high risk of heart disease, using the graph of HDL and LDL levels and own knowledge.
questions.answer: Even with HDL above 40, a man can still be at high risk because HDL = 43.5 gives much higher risk than 63.0 or 82.5, risk rises steeply as LDL rises, and other risk factors also raise heart disease risk.
steps: Graph: at HDL = 43.5 the risk of heart disease is far higher than at HDL = 63.0 or 82.5 at every LDL level, so HDL just above 40 gives much less protection than a high HDL.
At all HDL levels risk increases as the LDL level increases, and the lines for HDL = 24.4 and 43.5 rise steeply, so a man with high LDL still has a high risk.

Own knowledge: LDL carries cholesterol to the artery wall, where it builds up as atheroma (atherosclerosis), narrowing the coronary arteries and causing clots; HDL only removes some of this cholesterol.
Other risk factors are independent of HDL: smoking, high blood pressure, diet high in saturated fat and salt, obesity, inactivity, diabetes, age, sex and genetics.
Very high cholesterol can alter HDL so that it is less effective, so an HDL level above 40 does not guarantee protection.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure of HDL with altered HDL, shown in the diagrams.
questions.answer: Both are spherical particles with a phospholipid layer carrying ApoA-1 and polyunsaturated PC and a core of cholesteryl ester (CE), but altered HDL is much larger with a bigger CE core, fewer PC molecules and fewer types of protein.
steps: Similarities: both are roughly spherical; both have a surface phospholipid layer with long-chain polyunsaturated PC and the protein ApoA-1; both have a core of cholesteryl ester (CE).
Difference: altered HDL is much larger (greater diameter) than normal HDL.
Difference: altered HDL has a much larger core containing many more CE molecules.
Difference: HDL has several proteins (ApoA-1, ApoM, CRABP1, RBP4) but altered HDL shows only ApoA-1, and it has fewer long-chain polyunsaturated PC molecules in its surface layer.

questions.question: The antioxidant properties of altered HDL are reduced. Explain the effect this has on reducing the risk of heart disease.
questions.answer: Altered HDL can no longer prevent LDL being oxidised, so oxidised LDL builds up in the artery walls, forming atheroma and increasing the risk of heart disease.
steps: HDL normally has antioxidant properties that prevent LDL cholesterol being oxidised.
With reduced antioxidant action, LDL is oxidised more easily.
Oxidised LDL is taken up by macrophages and builds up as atheroma in artery walls.
This narrows the arteries and raises the risk of heart disease, so HDL is less able to lower risk.

questions.question: Complete the diagram with one lifestyle risk factor and one non-lifestyle risk factor for CVD.
questions.answer: Lifestyle: smoking (or diet, inactivity); non-lifestyle: age (or family history or sex).
steps: A lifestyle risk factor is one a person can change, such as smoking, diet, or lack of exercise.
A non-lifestyle risk factor is one a person cannot change, such as age, sex or family history.
Either a correct lifestyle factor and a correct non-lifestyle factor completes the diagram.
Lifestyle factors can be changed; non-lifestyle factors cannot.

questions.question: Describe the conclusions that can be made from the graph showing the effect of exercise on the relative risk of death from CVD.
questions.answer: Relative risk of death from CVD falls as the weekly energy spent on exercise increases, and the more vigorous the exercise the greater the fall.
steps: All three lines start at 1.0 at 4000 kJ per week and fall as energy used increases.
At 14000 kJ per week the relative risk is about 0.95 for light, 0.84 for moderate and 0.70 for vigorous exercise (reductions of 5%, 16% and 30%).

For the same energy expended, vigorous exercise gives the lowest risk (falls about 0.03 per 1000 kJ), moderate falls about 0.016 per 1000 kJ, and light exercise levels off after about 8000 kJ with little extra benefit.

questions.question: Explain how dietary antioxidants reduce the risk of CVD.
questions.answer: Antioxidants neutralise free radicals, stopping LDL cholesterol being oxidised, so less atheroma forms and the artery wall is protected.
steps: Free radicals are reactive molecules that damage cells and molecules.
Antioxidants donate electrons to free radicals, making them harmless.
This prevents LDL cholesterol being oxidised, so less oxidised LDL is taken up by macrophages.
Less atheroma forms and the endothelium is less damaged, so CVD risk falls.

questions.question: Devise a study to confirm that antioxidants reduce the risk of CVD.
questions.answer: A randomised, double-blind controlled trial giving antioxidant supplements or a placebo to large groups, controlling other variables, and comparing CVD incidence or markers.
steps: Recruit a large sample and randomly assign people to an antioxidant group or a placebo group.
Make the trial double-blind so neither participants nor researchers know the group.
Control variables such as diet, age, smoking and exercise.
Measure CVD events or markers (LDL oxidation, blood pressure) over a long period and compare the groups.

questions.question: Explain the effects on heart function after the coronary artery becomes completely blocked, using the energy graph; contraction stops at 8 minutes and cells begin to die at 20 minutes.
questions.answer: Without blood flow there is no oxygen, so aerobic respiration stops and energy release falls; contraction stops by 8 minutes as ATP runs out and the cells die from about 20 minutes.
steps: When the artery is blocked, oxygen and glucose no longer reach the heart muscle.
Aerobic respiration stops, so the energy (ATP) released by heart muscle cells falls.
Anaerobic respiration gives only a little ATP and lactic acid builds up, which lowers pH.
Without enough ATP the muscle cannot contract, so the heart stops contracting by 8 minutes.
After about 20 minutes the cells lack energy and begin to die, causing permanent damage to the heart muscle.

questions.question: How many of three statements about thromboplastin are correct: it is stored in platelets; it is an active enzyme; it is converted into thrombin? Options: A none, B one, C two, D three.
questions.answer: C two.
steps: Statement 1 is correct: thromboplastin is stored in platelets and released when they are activated.
Statement 2 is correct: thromboplastin is an active enzyme that converts prothrombin to thrombin.
Statement 3 is wrong: thromboplastin is not converted into thrombin; prothrombin is converted into thrombin.
Two statements are correct, so the answer is C.

questions.question: Deduce a safe range for the INR level, using the graph of INR against the risk of stroke and the risk of bleeding within the skull.
questions.answer: About 2.0 to 3.5 (1.8 to 3.5 is also acceptable).
steps: Below INR 1.8 the risk of stroke is high (very high at 1.3 or below and still raised at 1.4-1.7) because blood clots too easily.
Above 3.5 the risk of bleeding in the skull rises steeply (3.6-4.5, then very high above 4.5).
Between about 1.8 and 3.5 both risks are low and similar, with the lowest combined risk at 2.0-2.5, so a safe range is about 2.0 to 3.5.

questions.question: Explain how taking an anticoagulant such as warfarin can reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease.
questions.answer: Warfarin reduces the clotting process (vitamin K dependent clotting factors and thrombin formation), so fewer clots form that could block coronary or cerebral arteries, lowering the risk of heart attack and stroke.
steps: Warfarin blocks the production of clotting factors that depend on vitamin K, including prothrombin.
With less prothrombin, less thrombin is made, so less fibrin forms.
Fewer clots form in coronary or cerebral arteries, so blood flow is less likely to be blocked.
Lower clotting reduces the risk of heart attack and stroke, which are forms of CVD.

questions.question: A group of 1216 people were given warfarin, and 83.3% had no further health issues. Calculate the number of people given warfarin who had no further health issues.
questions.answer: 1013 people (1012.9 rounded).
steps: Number = 83.3% of 1216.
0.833 x 1216 = 1012.9, which is about 1013 people.
The number of people must be a whole number, so round the answer.

questions.question: A second study compared the result with people given a combination of warfarin and aspirin. Describe how this study should be carried out to produce a valid comparison.
questions.answer: Randomly assign similar patients after a first heart attack to warfarin, aspirin, or both, with the same dose, duration (four years) and follow-up, and measure the same outcomes.
steps: Recruit patients with a similar history (first heart attack) and similar characteristics such as age and smoking.
Randomly assign them to warfarin alone, aspirin alone or the combination, so groups are comparable.
Use the same dose and length of follow-up (four years) and record the same outcomes for each group.
Use a double-blind design where possible and control other factors, so only the drug treatment varies between groups.

questions.question: Which row of the table identifies one lifestyle factor and one non-lifestyle factor?
questions.answer: A
steps: Lifestyle factors can be changed; non-lifestyle factors cannot.
BMI can be changed by diet and exercise (lifestyle) and age cannot be changed (non-lifestyle), so row A is correct.
B, C and D each have a factor in the wrong column (for example gender and genetics cannot be changed, and inactivity and alcohol intake can).

questions.question: Explain why a person might have to take several types of drugs to reduce the risk of CVD.
questions.answer: CVD has several causes, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol and clotting, so each drug targets a different risk factor.
steps: CVD is caused by several interacting risk factors, not only one.
Antihypertensives lower blood pressure, statins lower blood cholesterol, and anticoagulants or platelet inhibitors reduce clotting.
A person may have more than one risk factor, so more than one drug is needed.
Each drug treats a different cause, so combined treatment reduces risk more effectively.

questions.question: Explain why antioxidants in the diet reduce the risk of CVD.
questions.answer: Antioxidants neutralise free radicals, which stops LDL cholesterol being oxidised, so less atheroma forms and the endothelium is protected.
steps: Free radicals damage molecules and the endothelium of blood vessels.
Antioxidants donate electrons to neutralise free radicals.
This prevents LDL cholesterol being oxidised, so it is less likely to be taken up and form atheroma.
Antioxidants stop the chain reactions that oxidise LDL.

questions.question: Some studies do not assess the nutritional quality of the participants' diets. Explain why the results of these studies have to be treated with caution.
questions.answer: Without measuring diet, other dietary factors (or lifestyle factors) could cause the effect, so the link to antioxidants cannot be confirmed; self-reported diets are also often inaccurate.
steps: If diet is not measured, other factors in the diet may be responsible for the result, which is a confounding variable.
The results may show association but cannot prove that antioxidants caused the change.
Participants' diets may be recorded inaccurately, so the data are less reliable.
So the conclusion that antioxidants reduce CVD risk must be treated with caution.

questions.question: Explain why changes in diet, other than antioxidants, can reduce the risk of CVD.
questions.answer: Reducing saturated fat lowers LDL cholesterol and reducing salt lowers blood pressure, so both reduce the chances of atheroma and CVD.
steps: Reducing saturated fat lowers LDL cholesterol in the blood.
Lower LDL means less cholesterol is deposited in artery walls, so less atheroma forms.
Reducing salt intake lowers blood pressure, which reduces strain on the arteries and heart.
Lower blood pressure and cholesterol together reduce the risk of CVD.

questions.question: Describe two conclusions that can be drawn from the study comparing perceived risk with actual risk of CVD.
questions.answer: People underestimate their actual risk for inactivity, high cholesterol and high blood pressure (perceived about 10 lower), but slightly overestimate being overweight; perceived and actual risk of smoking are close.
steps: Perceived v actual number of people: smoking 18 v 20; inactivity 25 v 35; overweight 58 v 55; high cholesterol 27 v 36; high blood pressure 25 v 36.
Conclusion 1: for four of the five factors the perceived risk is lower than the actual risk, with the biggest gaps for high blood pressure (11 people) and inactivity (10) and high cholesterol (9).

Conclusion 2: overweight is the only factor where more people perceived a risk than actually had it (58 v 55), and it is the most common risk factor; smoking has the closest match (2 people difference).

questions.question: Explain how this study should have been designed to allow valid conclusions to be made.
questions.answer: Use a large, representative sample, standard questions for perceived risk and standard clinical tests for actual risk, and measure both in the same people under the same conditions.
steps: Use a large and representative sample so the results can be generalised.
Ask every participant the same questions in the same way to measure perceived risk.
Measure actual risk with standard tests (blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking status) on the same people.
Compare the two measures in the same individuals, using the same criteria, to allow valid comparison.

questions.question: Explain why it is important that a person's perception of a risk is close to the actual risk.
questions.answer: People who underestimate their risk may not change their lifestyle or take medication, while those who overestimate may take unnecessary action; accurate perception leads to appropriate prevention.
steps: If a person underestimates their risk, they may not change diet, smoking or exercise habits.
Without changes, the risk of CVD stays high and they may not take preventive drugs.
If a person overestimates their risk, they may cause themselves stress or take unnecessary treatment.
An accurate perception lets people make sensible choices and get the right treatment.

questions.question: Calculate the 10-year risk of CVD for a 35-year-old woman with total cholesterol 242 mg dm-3, who is a smoker, and systolic blood pressure 132 mm Hg, using the Framingham point tables.
steps: Age 35 to 39: -3 points.
Total cholesterol 242 mg dm-3 is in the 240 to 279 band: +11; smoker: +9; systolic blood pressure 132 mm Hg is in the 130 to 139 band: +2.
Total = -3 + 11 + 9 + 2 = 19 points.
Table 2: 19 points gives a 10-year risk of 8%.

questions.question: Explain the lifestyle changes this woman could make to reduce her 10-year risk of CVD, using the information in the table.
questions.answer: Stop smoking first (saves 9 points: 19 to 10, so risk falls from 8% to below 4%), then lower cholesterol and blood pressure through diet and exercise.
steps: Stopping smoking removes the +9 points, taking the total from 19 to 10, below the lowest value in Table 2 (16 points = 4%), so risk falls from 8% to under 4%.
Lowering total cholesterol from 240-279 (+11) to 160-199 (+4) saves 7 points: eat less saturated fat and more fibre, and exercise more.
Lowering systolic blood pressure to below 120 mm Hg saves 2 points: eat less salt, lose weight, exercise and drink less alcohol.
Age (-3 points) is not a lifestyle factor and cannot be changed.

questions.question: Which pair of drugs may reduce the 10-year risk of CVD for the woman in part (b)(i) (35 years old, smoker, total cholesterol 242 mg dm-3, systolic blood pressure 132 mm Hg)? Options: A anticoagulants and statins, B anticoagulants and antihypertensives, C antihypertensives and platelet inhibitors, D antihypertensives and statins.
questions.answer: D antihypertensives and statins.
steps: The woman has high systolic blood pressure (132 mm Hg), which is treated with antihypertensives.
She has high total cholesterol (242 mg dm-3), which is treated with statins.
Anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors treat clotting rather than the two main risk factors shown, so D is the best answer.
Antihypertensives treat blood pressure and statins lower cholesterol.

questions.question: Suggest why this method of determining the 10-year risk of CVD may not be accurate.
questions.answer: The method uses only a limited set of risk factors, so it omits others such as family history, diabetes and diet, and the scores are based on population averages.
steps: The score uses only a few risk factors (cholesterol, smoking, blood pressure, age).
Important risk factors such as family history, diabetes, and stress are not included.
The points are based on population data, which may not match an individual.
Self-reported information may also be inaccurate, so the estimate may be wrong.

questions.question: Which row in the table describes the cholesterol content and antioxidant content of the Portfolio diet?
questions.answer: C: low cholesterol content and high antioxidant content.
steps: The Portfolio diet lowers LDL because it is mainly plant-based (nuts, soya protein, fibre, plant sterols), which contains little or no animal cholesterol, so the cholesterol content is low.
Plant foods such as fruit, vegetables and nuts are rich in antioxidants, so the antioxidant content is high.
Only row C has low cholesterol and high antioxidants.

questions.question: Name two other dietary risk factors that could be changed in this diet.
questions.answer: Salt (sodium) intake and saturated fat intake (or sugar intake).
steps: Dietary risk factors for CVD include high salt, high saturated fat and high sugar intake.
Reducing salt intake lowers blood pressure.
Reducing saturated fat lowers LDL cholesterol.
These dietary factors are established risk factors for CVD.

questions.question: Suggest why women with missing lifestyle information were removed from the initial group.
questions.answer: Their lifestyle factors cannot be known, so they cannot be properly compared with the other women, and the results would be less reliable.
steps: The study needs complete lifestyle information to compare the diet groups fairly.
Without it, lifestyle factors (such as smoking or exercise) that affect CVD cannot be controlled.
Removing them keeps the groups comparable and the results valid.
Missing data would bias the results.

questions.question: Give two reasons why some women may have given unrealistic estimates of their daily energy intake.
questions.answer: They may forget or misjudge what they ate (poor recall or portion size), or they may under-report or over-report to look healthier (social desirability).
steps: Many people find it hard to remember all the food they ate over a day.
Portion sizes are difficult to estimate accurately.
People may under-report intake, for example to avoid judgement or because they want to appear healthy.
Reasons include forgetting, misjudging portion sizes, and wanting to appear healthier.

questions.question: The women removed from the intermediary group had signs of CVD. Explain why these women were removed from the investigation.
questions.answer: The study investigates whether the diet affects the development of CVD, so women who already had CVD would distort the results and are removed.
steps: The investigation aims to see whether the diet reduces the development of CVD.
Women who already have CVD have a different starting risk, so they cannot show a new effect.
Including them would make the results less valid for the population at risk.
So they are removed to keep the study focused on those at risk of developing CVD.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage of all the women removed from this investigation, using the numbers in the diagram of the study.
Explain why a diet that is low in saturated fat is likely to reduce the risk of CVD.
questions.answer: Less saturated fat lowers blood LDL cholesterol, so less cholesterol is deposited in artery walls and less atheroma forms, reducing CVD risk.
steps: Saturated fats raise blood LDL cholesterol levels.
High LDL cholesterol leads to more cholesterol being deposited in artery walls.
This forms atheroma, which narrows arteries and can cause blockages.
A diet low in saturated fat keeps LDL low, so the atheroma and CVD risk are reduced.

questions.question: How many of the risk factors listed in the table are not influenced by lifestyle? Options: A 1, B 2, C 3, D 4.
questions.answer: A: 1 (age only).
steps: The factors in the table are age, blood pressure, smoking, total cholesterol and HDL cholesterol.
Blood pressure, smoking, total cholesterol and HDL cholesterol are all influenced by lifestyle (diet, exercise, smoking habit).
Only age is not influenced by lifestyle, so the answer is 1.

questions.question: Explain the effectiveness of the two risk assessment calculators in assessing risk, and whether other factors should be considered.
questions.answer: The calculators give a useful estimate using a few established risk factors, but they are limited by the information entered and omit other factors (such as family history, diet and stress), so other factors should be considered.
steps: Both calculators use established risk factors such as age, blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking, so they give a useful estimate.
They rely on self-reported information, which may be inaccurate, so the result can be wrong.
They are based on population data, so they may not predict risk accurately for every individual.
Important factors such as family history, ethnicity, diabetes, diet and stress are often not included.
Including more factors would make the estimate more accurate, and a doctor should consider them in a full assessment.
So the calculators are a useful screening tool but should be used alongside clinical judgement.

questions.question: Explain why the information entered by a person may lead to an underestimate of their 10-year risk of developing CVD.
questions.answer: People may under-report smoking, alcohol, diet or inactivity, or not know their blood pressure or cholesterol, so the calculator gives too low a risk.
steps: People may not know their exact blood pressure or cholesterol level.
People may under-report unhealthy habits such as smoking, drinking or poor diet.
The calculator uses the entered values, so incorrect inputs give a lower risk score.
The 10-year risk is therefore underestimated.

questions.question: Suggest why these two risk calculators may not be suitable for everybody to use.
questions.answer: They are based on data from certain populations (age, sex, ethnicity), so they may not be accurate for people outside those groups or with existing conditions.
steps: The calculators were developed using data from particular groups of people.
They may not be accurate for different ages, sexes or ethnic groups.
People who already have CVD or diabetes may need different assessment.
So the results may be misleading for those people.

questions.question: Suggest why these risk calculators estimate the 10-year risk of developing CVD.
questions.answer: CVD develops over many years, so a 10-year timescale is a practical period to guide prevention and treatment decisions.
steps: CVD usually develops slowly over many years.
A 10-year period is long enough to show meaningful risk but short enough to be useful.
Doctors can use this to decide whether preventive treatment, such as statins or antihypertensives, is needed.
The timescale matches how risk builds up over years.

questions.question: CVD kills 17.9 million people per year, which is 31% of all global deaths. Calculate how many global deaths there are in one year, in standard form.
questions.answer: 5.77 x 10^7 deaths (about 57.7 million).
steps: Total deaths = 17.9 million / 0.31.
17.9 / 0.31 = 57.74, so total deaths = 57.74 million.
In standard form this is 5.77 x 10^7.
Check: 57.7 million x 0.31 is about 17.9 million.

questions.question: It is predicted that by 2030 more than 22.2 million people will die each year from CVD. Suggest how this prediction was made.
questions.answer: By extrapolating past trends in CVD death numbers (using statistical modelling of population growth and ageing).
steps: Data on CVD deaths over past years are collected.
A trend line or statistical model is fitted to these data.
The trend is extended (extrapolated) to 2030.
Population growth and ageing are included in the model to predict the future number of deaths.

questions.question: Explain why eating ginger rhizomes, which have high levels of antioxidants, may help to prevent CVD.
questions.answer: Antioxidants in ginger neutralise free radicals, so LDL cholesterol is less likely to be oxidised, reducing atheroma formation and damage to the endothelium.
steps: Antioxidants donate electrons to neutralise free radicals.
This prevents oxidation of LDL cholesterol.
Oxidised LDL is less likely to build up as atheroma in artery walls.
Less atheroma and less endothelial damage reduce the risk of CVD.

questions.question: Suggest why ginger can be eaten to prevent CVD even though its effectiveness has not been thoroughly tested.
questions.answer: Ginger is a common food with known antioxidant properties and is generally safe to eat in normal amounts, so there is little risk in including it in the diet.
steps: Ginger is a food that has been eaten for a long time with no known harm at normal amounts.
It contains antioxidants that are known to be beneficial for the heart.
So eating it is low risk even before its effect is fully proven.
Eating ginger is low risk, so it can be included before its effectiveness is fully known.

questions.question: Explain how a study should be designed to collect valid and repeatable data to show the effectiveness of ginger in preventing CVD.
questions.answer: Use a large randomised, double-blind controlled trial with a ginger group and a placebo control group, controlled variables, and repeated measurements of CVD markers over time.
steps: Recruit a large, representative sample of people at similar risk of CVD.
Randomly assign them to a ginger group or a placebo (control) group.
Make the trial double-blind so neither participants nor researchers know the group, to avoid bias.
Control variables such as diet, age, smoking and exercise, and use the same dose and duration for all.
Measure CVD markers (blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, endothelial function) at the start and repeatedly, using standard methods so the results are repeatable.
Use statistical analysis to compare the two groups.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage increase in the thickness of the artery wall where the plaque is located, measured along the line X-Y on the photograph.
questions.answer: About 200% (the wall at the plaque is about three times as thick as the normal wall; accept about 150 to 250% depending on measurement).
steps: Use a ruler along the line X-Y: measure the wall thickness at the plaque (X to the edge of the lumen) and the normal wall thickness on the opposite side (edge of the lumen to Y).
On this photograph the wall at the plaque is about 3 times as thick as the normal wall (for example about 36 mm v 12 mm on the printed page; there is no scale bar, so use the same units for both).
Percentage increase = (thickness at plaque - normal thickness) / normal thickness x 100.

questions.question: Explain how atherosclerosis can result in damage to the heart muscle.
questions.answer: Atheroma narrows the coronary arteries, reducing oxygen supply to heart muscle; plaques can rupture and cause clots that block the artery, killing muscle cells in a heart attack.
steps: Atheroma builds up in the walls of the coronary arteries and narrows the lumen.
Less blood flows through, so less oxygen and glucose reach the heart muscle, causing angina during exertion.
Plaques can rupture, releasing material that triggers a blood clot (thrombus).
A clot can completely block the coronary artery, so heart muscle cells die (heart attack), leaving scar tissue and reducing pumping ability.

questions.question: Assess the contribution of the lipoproteins LDL and HDL to the risk of developing CVD, using Graph 1 (total cholesterol and death risk) and Graph 2 (LDL size and ratio of total cholesterol to HDL).
questions.answer: LDL and HDL both make a major contribution: total cholesterol and a high total cholesterol:HDL ratio, especially with small LDL particles, are linked to more CVD, but other factors also matter and the graphs show correlation only.
steps: Graph 1: in all four populations the percentage of deaths from CVD rises as total cholesterol rises (for example Northern Europe 14.5% at 5.0 mmol dm-3 to 30% at 8.3; United States 10.8% at 4.85 to 26% at 7.75).

But total cholesterol is not the only factor: at about 5 mmol dm-3 deaths differ by region (Northern Europe about 14.5%, USA about 11%, Southern Europe inland about 8.5%, Mediterranean about 3.5%), so diet, lifestyle and other risk factors also affect CVD.
Graph 2: a high ratio of total cholesterol to HDL (above 6) raises relative risk of CVD for both LDL sizes: small LDL 1.25 to 4.9 (about 4 times) and large LDL 1.0 to 1.7.
Small LDL is more harmful than large LDL: at a ratio above 6 the relative risk is 4.9 v 1.7 (about 2.9 times), perhaps because small LDL enters the artery wall and is oxidised more easily.

Own knowledge: LDL carries cholesterol to tissues and deposits it in artery walls as atheroma, leading to atherosclerosis, blood clots and CHD; HDL carries cholesterol away to the liver, so it is protective.

Overall, lipoproteins make a large contribution (more LDL, especially small LDL, and less HDL raise risk), but the data show correlation not cause, and smoking, blood pressure, obesity, age and genetics also contribute.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure of an unsaturated fatty acid with the structure of a saturated fatty acid.
questions.answer: Both have a carboxyl group and a hydrocarbon chain; a saturated fatty acid has only single C-C bonds (straight chain), while an unsaturated one has at least one C=C double bond that causes a kink.
steps: Similarity: both are fatty acids with a hydrocarbon chain and a carboxyl (COOH) group at one end.
Contrast: a saturated fatty acid has only single C-C bonds, so its chain is straight.
Contrast: an unsaturated fatty acid has one or more C=C double bonds, which put kinks in the chain.
The kinks stop unsaturated fatty acids packing tightly, so they are liquid at room temperature.

questions.question: The group had 41 701 men and 68 786 women. Which is the ratio of men to women? Options: A 0.6:1, B 1:0.6, C 1:2, D 2:1.
steps: Ratio of men to women = 41 701 / 68 786.
41 701 / 68 786 = 0.606, so the ratio is about 0.6 : 1.
This matches option A.
Check: 0.6 x 68 786 is close to 41 701.

questions.question: Describe the questions that need to be in the questionnaire so that appropriate information can be gathered for this investigation about avocados and CHD, and give reasons for choosing them.
questions.answer: Ask how often avocados and other animal and plant foods are eaten (with portion sizes), plus smoking, exercise, age and existing health, with reasons linked to how each affects CHD risk.
steps: Ask how often and how much avocado is eaten each week, because the study tests the effect of avocado intake.
Ask how often animal products and other foods are eaten, because avocados replace them and the change in diet must be recorded.
Ask about other risk factors such as smoking, alcohol, exercise and existing conditions, because these affect CHD and must be controlled.
Use closed questions with set portion sizes to make answers comparable and reduce recall error.
Repeat the questionnaire every four years to track changes in diet over time.
Reasons: each question gathers data on a variable that could change the CHD outcome, so the results can be properly compared.

questions.question: Comment on the validity of the methods used in this investigation into avocados and CHD.
questions.answer: Self-reported questionnaires may be inaccurate, the study is observational so it cannot prove cause, and confounding factors must be controlled; the long follow-up is a strength.
steps: Questionnaires rely on recall and self-reporting, which can be inaccurate, reducing validity.
It is an observational study, so it shows association rather than proof that avocados cause the change.
Other factors such as smoking, exercise and existing health must be adjusted for to avoid confounding.
The long follow-up over 30 years and repeated questionnaires are strengths that improve reliability.

questions.question: Name one other obesity indicator, apart from body mass index (BMI).
questions.answer: Waist-to-hip ratio (or waist circumference or skinfold thickness).
steps: Obesity indicators measure body size or fat distribution.
Waist-to-hip ratio compares waist and hip measurements.
Waist circumference and skinfold thickness are also valid indicators.
Waist-to-hip ratio is a measure of fat distribution.

questions.question: Which is the BMI of a person with a mass of 65 kg and a height of 165 cm? Options: A 23, B 24, C 39, D 40.
steps: Convert height to metres: 165 cm = 1.65 m.
65 / 2.7225 = 23.9, which rounds to 24, so the answer is B.
Check: 24 is the nearest option to 23.9.

questions.question: Which describes the body mass of a person who is obese? The four options (A to D) use inequality symbols that are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: B: BMI >= 30
steps: A person with a BMI of 25 to below 30 is overweight, so obesity starts at a BMI of 30 and includes 30.
Option B (BMI greater than or equal to 30) is therefore correct; A leaves out exactly 30, and C and D describe lower BMI values.

questions.question: State two ways in which a person could lose weight.
questions.answer: Eat fewer calories (reduce energy intake) and increase physical activity (exercise).
steps: Weight is lost when energy intake is less than energy used.
Reducing food intake or choosing lower-energy food reduces energy intake.
Increasing physical activity uses more energy through respiration, so more fat is used.
Both methods reduce energy intake or increase energy use, creating a negative energy balance.

questions.question: Which row of the table describes the action of amylase in breaking down amylose into maltose?
questions.answer: C: hydrolysis of 1-4 glycosidic bonds.
steps: Amylase breaks amylose into maltose by hydrolysis, which uses water to break the bonds; condensation is the reverse reaction.
Amylose is a chain of glucose joined by 1-4 glycosidic bonds, which amylase breaks (1-6 bonds are the branch points in amylopectin).
So the row is hydrolysis, 1-4, which is C.

questions.question: People with low levels of amylase in their saliva lost weight more easily. Suggest why.
questions.answer: Less starch is broken down into maltose and glucose, so less energy is absorbed from the food, reducing energy intake.
steps: Amylase starts the digestion of starch (amylose) into maltose in the mouth.
With low amylase, less starch is broken down in the mouth.
Larger starch molecules pass further along the gut where fewer enzymes act, so less glucose is absorbed.
Less energy is absorbed, so the person takes in fewer calories and loses weight more easily.

questions.question: Explain why the finding that people with greater weight loss had bacteria with increased rates of replication can be described as a positive correlation.
questions.answer: As one variable (weight loss) increases, the other variable (rate of bacterial replication) also increases, so the two variables change in the same direction.
steps: A positive correlation means that as one variable increases, the other also increases.
Here, greater weight loss goes with higher rates of bacterial replication.
Both variables increase together, so it is a positive correlation (but not proof of cause).
Both variables increase together, which is the definition of positive correlation.

questions.question: Suggest why the rate of replication of the bacteria could affect weight loss.
questions.answer: Gut bacteria affect how much energy is extracted from food and how fat is stored, so faster replication can change the energy absorbed and the amount of weight lost.
steps: Bacteria in the digestive system break down some food components that the body cannot digest alone.
Their activity changes how much energy is released and absorbed from food.
Faster replication means more bacteria and a greater effect on energy absorption.
So the energy taken in, and therefore weight loss, may change.

questions.topic: Mean Rate of Monacolin K Production
questions.question: Calculate the mean rate of production of monacolin K in the culture over the 45-day period, to two decimal places.
questions.answer: 7.56 mg per 100 g of rice per day
steps: From the graph, the concentration of monacolin K is 0 at the start and about 340 mg per 100 g at 45 days.
Mean rate = change in concentration / time = (340 - 0) / 45.
= 7.56 mg per 100 g of rice per day (to 2 decimal places).

questions.topic: Limits of Red Yeast Rice Studies
questions.question: Discuss the limitations of using the four studies, and the two graphs of LDL cholesterol levels, to draw conclusions about the effects of red yeast rice on lipid levels.
questions.answer: The studies are not directly comparable and show no consistent dose effect, the graphs show small groups, overlapping error bars, only short-term effects and incomplete data, so firm conclusions on RYR and lipid levels cannot be drawn.
steps: Table: the four studies use different doses (340, 1200 and 2400 mg per day) and give inconsistent results: 340 mg lowers LDL by 21-24% yet 2400 mg lowers it by only 23% (study 3) or 32% (study 4), and 1200 mg gives 34% (study 2) or 23% (study 4); RYR products probably vary in monacolin K content.
HDL data are missing for studies 3 and 4 and conflict for 1 and 2 (no change v +18); sample sizes, duration, participants and controls are not given, and some results are ranges rather than means.
Graph 1: only 10 weeks with small groups (n = 21 or 22); the 100 mg and 200 mg lines are similar and error bars are large and overlap, so a dose effect cannot be shown.
LDL returned to about the control level within 2 weeks of stopping RYR, so the effect is short-lived, and there is no long-term data on LDL or on CVD events.

Graph 2: the time axis has no values or units, sample size and what the error bars show are not given, and the error bars overlap (for example 4.1 and 4.8) so differences may not be significant; the LDL unit and scale differ from Graph 1.
No statistical tests, different populations and possible side effects and diet are not reported, so correlation and cause cannot be separated.

questions.question: Name two possible side effects of being treated with statins.
questions.answer: Muscle pain (myopathy) and liver damage (or kidney problems, or digestive upset).
steps: Statins can cause muscle pain or weakness (myopathy).
They can affect liver function, shown by raised liver enzymes.
Other side effects include digestive problems and, rarely, kidney damage.
Symptoms like these are monitored in clinical trials.

questions.question: Describe how an investigation could be designed to identify any side effects of treatment with monacolin K.
questions.answer: Use a randomised, double-blind trial with a placebo control group, give the same dose over a set period, and monitor symptoms and blood tests such as liver enzymes and muscle markers.
steps: Randomly assign participants to a monacolin K group or a placebo control group.
Make the trial double-blind so neither participants nor researchers know which group is which.
Give the same dose for the same period to each group, and record all symptoms and side effects.
Take blood samples at intervals to measure liver enzymes and muscle markers (creatine kinase) and compare with the control.

questions.question: Suggest two problems when assessing possible side effects resulting from treatment with monacolin K in an investigation.
questions.answer: Participants may report side effects inaccurately (self-report bias or placebo effect), and other medicines or conditions may cause the same symptoms (confounding).
steps: Side effects such as pain or tiredness are subjective, so they are difficult to measure accurately.
Participants who know they are taking a drug may report more or fewer symptoms (placebo or nocebo effect).
Other drugs or health conditions may cause the same symptoms, so the cause may be wrongly identified.
Controlling variables helps isolate the side effects of the drug.

questions.question: Which molecule, released from platelets, results in blood clotting? Options: A fibrinogen, B prothrombin, C thrombin, D thromboplastin.
questions.answer: D thromboplastin.
steps: Platelets release thromboplastin when the vessel is damaged.
Thromboplastin converts prothrombin into thrombin, which starts the clotting process.
Fibrinogen, prothrombin and thrombin are plasma proteins rather than platelet products, so A, B and C are wrong.
Thromboplastin acts on prothrombin to start the clotting process.

questions.question: Which pair of molecules are enzymes in their active form? Options: A fibrinogen and prothrombin, B prothrombin and thrombin, C thrombin and thromboplastin, D thromboplastin and prothrombin.
questions.answer: C thrombin and thromboplastin.
steps: Thrombin is an active enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin.
Thromboplastin is an active enzyme that converts prothrombin to thrombin.
Prothrombin and fibrinogen are inactive precursors, so options A, B and D are wrong.
Active enzymes have a correctly shaped active site that can bind their substrate.

questions.question: Which molecule found in the blood is insoluble? Options: A fibrin, B fibrinogen, C prothrombin, D thromboplastin.
questions.answer: A fibrin.
steps: Fibrinogen is a soluble plasma protein.
Fibrin is formed from fibrinogen as insoluble threads forming the clot mesh.
So the answer is A.
Fibrin is insoluble because it forms long fibres.

questions.question: Suggest why a pulmonary embolism, where a clot blocks the pulmonary artery, can cause difficulty in breathing and a rapid heart rate.
questions.answer: The clot blocks blood flow to the lungs, so less gas exchange happens; low oxygen causes faster breathing and the heart beats faster to keep oxygen delivery up.
steps: A clot in the pulmonary artery blocks blood flow to part of the lungs.
Less blood reaches the alveoli, so less oxygen enters the blood and less carbon dioxide is removed.
Low blood oxygen and high carbon dioxide are detected, causing faster breathing and a feeling of breathlessness.
The heart beats faster to try to maintain oxygen delivery to the body.

questions.question: Discuss whether the finding that hibernating bears produce less HSP47, a protein involved in binding platelets to damaged blood vessels, could be useful to humans.
questions.answer: It could help develop drugs that reduce platelet binding and lower DVT risk, but platelets must still seal real wounds, so the effect must be controlled and tested in humans.
steps: HSP47 helps platelets bind to damaged blood vessels, which is part of clot formation.
Bears with less HSP47 may form fewer clots during inactivity, suggesting a target for DVT drugs.
Reducing binding too much could increase bleeding, so the effect must be controlled carefully.
Human trials would be needed before any treatment could be developed.

questions.question: Complete the passage about prothrombin: it is transported in the plasma of a human; it is converted into thrombin by an enzyme; the substrate for thrombin is a named molecule.
questions.answer: Plasma; thromboplastin (prothrombin activator); fibrinogen.
steps: Prothrombin is a soluble protein carried in the blood plasma.
Thromboplastin (prothrombin activator) converts prothrombin into the active enzyme thrombin.
Thrombin acts on its substrate fibrinogen, converting it into insoluble fibrin.
Prothrombin is made in the liver, so it is carried in plasma.

questions.question: Which pair of drugs is used to treat patients who have short blood clotting times? Options: A anticoagulants and antihypertensives, B anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors, C antihypertensives and statins, D platelet inhibitors and statins.
questions.answer: B anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors.
steps: A short clotting time means the blood clots too easily, so clotting must be slowed.
Anticoagulants slow the clotting cascade.
Platelet inhibitors stop platelets clumping together.
Antihypertensives and statins do not directly reduce clotting, so B is correct.

questions.question: A person with a PT of 8.5 seconds was treated to increase it to 10 seconds. Calculate the percentage increase in PT.
steps: Increase = 10 - 8.5 = 1.5 seconds.
Percentage increase = (1.5 / 8.5) x 100 = 17.6 %.
Percentage increase is the change divided by the original value, multiplied by 100.
Check: the answer is positive, as the PT increased.

questions.question: The world population at the end of 2023 was 8 078 799 080, and about 70% were adults. Estimate the number of adults in standard form.
questions.answer: 5.66 x 10^9 adults (about 5.66 billion).
steps: Adults = 70% of the population = 0.70 x 8 078 799 080.
Expressed to 3 significant figures in standard form, this is 5.66 x 10^9.
Standard form 5.66 x 10^9 has 3 significant figures, matching the data.

questions.question: Give two other examples of a healthy lifestyle, apart from good oral hygiene, that can help reduce the risk of CVD.
questions.answer: Not smoking, and taking regular exercise (or a healthy balanced diet, or limiting alcohol).
steps: Not smoking reduces damage to the endothelium and lowers blood pressure.
Regular exercise helps control weight and lowers blood pressure and cholesterol.
A healthy diet low in saturated fat and salt also reduces CVD risk.
Each example is a lifestyle change that lowers CVD risk factors.

questions.question: Give the meaning of the term correlation.
questions.answer: A relationship between two variables in which they change together, which does not by itself prove that one causes the other.
steps: A correlation is a statistical link between two variables.
The variables may increase together (positive) or one may increase as the other decreases (negative).
A correlation does not show that one variable causes the change in the other.
Correlation does not prove cause and effect.

questions.question: Explain why it was important that all the people in the study had similar blood pressure within a healthy range.
questions.answer: Blood pressure affects endothelial damage, so keeping it similar and healthy means that any difference in damage is due to the neutrophils, not blood pressure.
steps: Blood pressure itself can damage the endothelium of arteries.
If blood pressure differed between volunteers, it would be a confounding variable.
Keeping blood pressure similar and healthy ensures that the differences in endothelial damage are caused by neutrophils.
This makes the results valid and the comparison fair.

questions.question: Calculate the blood pressure of a person with systolic blood pressure 11.0 kPa and diastolic blood pressure 6.7 kPa, using the formula given in the text.
questions.answer: 8.13 kPa
steps: Blood pressure = (SBP + 2 x DBP) / 3.

questions.question: Explain why damage to endothelial cells might be an indication that a person is at risk of CVD.
questions.answer: Damaged endothelium cannot control blood vessel diameter or stop clotting properly, so cholesterol and platelets can build up, forming atheroma and increasing CVD risk.
steps: The endothelium is a smooth lining that stops platelets sticking and controls blood vessel diameter.
When damaged, it releases fewer protective chemicals such as nitric oxide and allows platelets to stick.
Cholesterol and inflammatory cells then enter the artery wall and form atheroma.
This narrows and stiffens the arteries, which indicates raised risk of CVD.

questions.question: Comment on the relationships between the number of neutrophils and the proportion of healthy endothelial cells of males and females in this study, using the graphs.
questions.answer: There is a negative relationship in both sexes: more neutrophils in saliva goes with fewer healthy endothelial cells, with all high-count values below about 10 a.u. and lots of scatter at low counts.
steps: Top graph: as neutrophils rise from 0 to 6.5 x 10^4 cells cm-3 the proportion of healthy endothelial cells tends to fall, in both males and females (a negative correlation).
Bottom graph: at a low count (2.5 or below) the proportion of healthy cells ranges from 0 to about 19.5, but at a high count (above 2.5) all values are lower, between about 1.5 and 9.5.
Males and females show the same trend, and there is no clear difference between the sexes (more of the high-count points are female, 5 v 3).
There is a wide scatter at low counts (for example 0 to 19 near 1.5), so neutrophil number is not the only factor; the relationship is a correlation only, with a small sample and no statistical test.

questions.question: Describe the differences between cardiovascular disease (CVD) and coronary heart disease (CHD).
questions.answer: CVD is a general term for diseases of the heart and blood vessels, including stroke; CHD is a specific type of CVD in which the coronary arteries are narrowed by atheroma.
steps: CVD covers all diseases of the heart and blood vessels, including CHD, stroke and peripheral arterial disease.
CHD is a specific form of CVD affecting the coronary arteries that supply the heart muscle.
CHD is caused by atheroma narrowing the coronary arteries, leading to angina or heart attack.
CVD is the umbrella term; CHD is one type of CVD.

questions.question: Calculate the BMI of a woman who is 165 cm tall with a mass of 68 kg.
questions.answer: 25.0 kg per m squared (25.0 to 3 significant figures).
steps: Height = 1.65 m, so height squared = 2.7225 m^2.
BMI = mass / height^2 = 68 / 2.7225.
Check: a BMI of 25 is at the lower bound of overweight.

questions.question: Calculate the waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) of a woman with a waist circumference of 85 cm and a hip measurement of 101 cm.
steps: WHR = waist circumference / hip measurement = 85 / 101.
Expressed as a ratio to 1 this is 0.84 : 1.
The WHR is compared with reference values to assess risk.

questions.question: Explain why high blood pressure is a risk factor for CVD.
questions.answer: High blood pressure damages the endothelium and artery walls, promotes atheroma and makes the heart work harder, which can lead to heart attack or stroke.
steps: High pressure damages the endothelium of arteries, making them more likely to develop atheroma.
Damaged, thickened arteries are narrower and less flexible.
The heart has to pump harder against high pressure, increasing workload and risk of heart failure.
High pressure can also rupture weakened vessels, causing a stroke.

questions.question: Name two other risk factors that might have been recorded as present or absent but not measured in the study.
questions.answer: Smoking status and family history of CVD (or diabetes).
steps: Smoking is recorded as present or absent (smoker or non-smoker).
Family history of heart disease is recorded as present or absent.
Diabetes status is also a yes-or-no factor that is commonly recorded.
Both are yes/no characteristics recorded in the questionnaire.

questions.question: Discuss the usefulness of BMI and WHR in predicting death from CVD and CHD, using the graphs of BMI and WHR of men and women who died.
questions.answer: WHR is the better predictor of death from both CVD and CHD, because it shows a steady rise in risk with increasing WHR in both sexes, while BMI gives an irregular pattern, especially in women.
steps: WHR: percentage of deaths from CVD rises steadily and steeply at higher WHR (men about 13% at 1.05 or more; women about 9% at 0.94-0.99), and the same pattern is seen for CHD, in both sexes.

BMI: CVD deaths in men fall from about 2.7% (below 20) to 1.5% (20-24.9) then rise to about 10% at 40 or more; in women they stay below 4% and are irregular (drop at 35-39.9); for CHD, men reach 4.6% at 35-39.9 but women stay at 2% or less, so BMI is a weaker predictor.
BMI does not distinguish fat from muscle or show where fat is stored, whereas WHR shows abdominal fat, which is more strongly linked to CVD.
Both are only associations, and other risk factors were not controlled, so both are useful but WHR is better.
